nodes.name: Solvothermal Synthesis of Ni-FeWO4@WO3/NF-1
nodes.procedure: The Ni-FeWO4@WO3/NF-1 self-supporting electrode was prepared through a facile solvothermal process. The Fe^{3+} is reduced by cyclohexanol and NF to generate Ni^{2+} and Fe^{2+}. Subsequently, Ni^{2+} and Fe^{2+} react with dissolved WO4^{2-} to form a tungstate solid solution (Ni-FeWO4). Due to the limited solubility of Na2WO4·2H2O in cyclohexanol, some undissolved Na2WO4·2H2O decomposes and deposits as WO3 on the surface of tungstate solid solution.
nodes.source_text: As described in Figure 1a, the Ni-FeWO4@WO3/NF-1 self-supporting electrode was prepared through a facile solvothermal process. The Fe^{3+} is reduced by cyclohexanol and NF to generate Ni^{2+} and Fe^{2+}. Subsequently, Ni^{2+} and Fe^{2+} react with dissolved WO4^{2-} to form a tungstate solid solution (Ni-FeWO4). Due to the limited solubility of Na2WO4·2H2O in cyclohexanol, some undissolved Na2WO4·2H2O decomposes and deposits as WO3 on the surface of tungstate solid solution.

nodes.characterization_summary: Characteristic diffraction peaks of FeWO₄ and hexagonal phase WO₃ are observed; Ni-FeWO₄ peaks exhibit slight high-angle shift compared to FeWO₄ (JCPDS 74-1130), WO₃ matches JCPDS 33-1387.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern shows the characteristic diffraction peaks of both FeWO₄ and hexagonal phase WO₃ (Figure 1b). Particularly, the diffraction peaks of Ni-FeWO₄ exhibit a slight high-angle shift compared with that of FeWO₄ (JCPDS 74-1130), while the diffraction peaks of WO₃ match well with JCPDS 33-1387.

nodes.characterization_summary: TEM confirms nanosheets stacked on sheet-like substrate; AC-TEM shows clear bridged interfaces with matched lattice between Ni-FeWO₄-1 and WO₃.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In Figure 1e, the transmission electron microscopy (TEM) image of Ni-FeWO₄@WO₃/NF-1 confirms that the nanosheets were stacked on the larger sheet-like substrate.

nodes.characterization_summary: Aberration-corrected TEM exhibits clear bridged interfaces with tight lattice contact between (200) plane of WO₃ and (-111) plane of Ni-FeWO₄-1.
nodes.evidence_snippet: An imaging of the interface between the nanosheets and the sheet-like substrate is captured using aberration-corrected transmission electron microscopy (AC-TEM) as shown in Figure 1f, which exhibits clear bridged interfaces with matched lattice between Ni-FeWO₄-1 and WO₃.

nodes.characterization_summary: EDS mapping reveals uniform distribution of W, Fe, Ni, and O elements.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Moreover, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping reveals the uniform distribution of W, Fe, Ni, and O, which further confirms the successful introduction of Ni in the composite (Figure 1h).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni 2p region shows 0.4 eV downward shift; Fe 2p region shows 0.7 eV shift toward low binding energy compared to Ni-FeWO₄-1; spin-splitting peaks dominated by Ni²⁺.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The significant shifts in the binding energy of the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) prove that the built-in electric field results in low oxidation states of Fe and Ni in the tungstate. Ni-FeWO₄@WO₃-1 shows a downward shift of 0.4 eV of the binding energy in the Ni 2p region compared with that of Ni-FeWO₄-1 (Figure 2a; and Figure S8, Supporting Information).

nodes.characterization_summary: Pre-K-edges of Ni and Fe shift toward low energy without significant shape changes after coupling with WO₃.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In the X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES), the pre-K-edges of Fe and Ni correspond to the electron transition from 1s to 3d orbitals, reflecting their coordination structures and oxidation states. The pre-K-edges of Ni and Fe shift toward low energy without significant shape changes after being coupled with WO₃ (Figure 2c,d).

nodes.characterization_summary: Prolonged Ni-O and Fe-O bond lengths in Ni-FeWO₄@WO₃-1.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Furthermore, the extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) shows the prolonged Ni-O and Fe-O bond length in Ni-FeWO₄@WO₃-1 providing further evidence (Figure 2e,f).

nodes.characterization_summary: WO₃ exhibits higher Fermi level (2.01 eV) compared to Ni-FeWO₄-1 (0.14 eV).
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Figure 2g, n-type semiconductor WO₃ exhibits a higher Fermi level (2.01 eV) compared with that of Ni FeWO₄-1 (0.14 eV) in the ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) spectra.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-FeWO₄@WO₃/NF-1 shows smallest charge transfer resistance of 0.33 Ω.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Furthermore, Ni-FeWO₄@WO₃/NF-1 shows the smallest charge transfer resistance in the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) Nyquist curves (0.33 Ω, Table S2, Supporting Information), providing the fastest charge transfer (Figure 3d; and Figure S13c, Supporting Information).

nodes.characterization_summary: Electric double-layer capacitance C_dl increases from 166 mF/cm² to 207 mF/cm² for Ni-FeWO₄@WO₃/NF-1 after coupling with WO₃.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The electric double-layer capacitance (C_dl) of Ni-FeWO₄/NF-1 also increases from 166 to 207 mF cm⁻² after being coupled with WO₃ (Figure 3e; and Figure S14, Supporting Information).

nodes.characterization_summary: Tungstate and WO₃ signals (810 cm⁻¹) persist at high potentials; FeOOH peaks maintained under OER potentials.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The in situ Raman spectra of Ni-FeWO₄@WO₃-1 show the consistent presence of tungstate and WO₃ signals (810 cm⁻¹) at high potentials, verifying the structural stability of Ni-FeWO₄@WO₃-1 (Figure 4b).

nodes.characterization_summary: WO₃: -33.8 mV; Ni-FeWO₄-1: -2.39 mV; Ni-FeWO₄@WO₃-1: -22.2 mV.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Figure S25 (Supporting Information) and 4f, WO₃ exhibits a negative Zeta potential (-33.8 mV), while Ni-FeWO₄-1 has a nearly neutral surface (-2.39 mV). Ni-FeWO₄@WO₃-1 exhibits a higher surface electronegativity (-22.2 mV) than that of Ni-FeWO₄-1.
